page: Amazon Web Services u-3tb1.56xlarge is a high-memory bare-metal caliber instance running on the AWS Nitro System, architected primarily for memory-intensive enterprise environments. It features 224 dedicated vCPUs derived from 112 physical cores of Intel Xeon Platinum 8176M processors operating at 2.1 GHz on the x86_64 architecture. The system is provisioned with 3,072 GB of DDR4 memory running at 3 GHz, offering an allocation of approximately 13.71 GB per virtual core. Storage is strictly external, as no local disk is bundled, and network connectivity is anchored by a baseline bandwidth of 50 Gbps without any complimentary public IPv4 addresses. Dedicated GPUs are absent in this configuration.

Benchmark outcomes show that the instance scales exceptionally well in highly concurrent compute tasks while showing typical limitations in per-core performance. The stress-ng multi-core benchmark places the instance in the top tier with a score of 169,737.36, complemented by a strong PassMark CPU score of 82,144.01 and top-tier PassMark CPU extended instruction execution. Conversely, single-threaded metrics reflect the lower base clock speed of the Xeon 8176M, with Geekbench single-core scoring 1,056.0 and stress-ng single-core performance landing in the middle tier. In-memory operations show stellar scaling, reflected by a top-tier Redis SET benchmark achieving 145.62 million operations per second and uncached read memory bandwidth exceeding 404 GB/sec.

Given the vast allocation of 3 TB of RAM paired with 224 vCPUs, the instance represents high resource density for enterprise environments requiring massive contiguous memory. Cost efficiency stems from consolidating large monolithic architectures rather than single-threaded speed efficiency. The lack of integrated local NVMe storage requires external network block storage for persistence, which makes the 50 Gbps network profile critical. This instance is best suited for large-scale in-memory databases like SAP HANA, massive enterprise caches, and memory-bound transactional data processing workloads.
